prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. passages.text: and acceptance criteria shall be formulated in accordance with design requirements and site conditions. 1.1.5 Maintenance Key Points 1. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority.  Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:

Justice

- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort

- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability

Selected Indicators:

 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Sidewalks shall be firm and level, with no cracks, missing bricks, damage, or other defects; joint widths shall be uniform and joints fully filled. All manhole covers shall be flush with the sidewalk elevation and in good condition, and their strength must meet sidewalk traffic requirements. 2. Sidewalks must have a base course and bedding course of sufficient strength. For settlement, breakage, or damage caused by insufficient base-course strength, the base course shall first be reinforced before the surface blocks are repaved. 3. To ensure safe pedestrian passage in rain and snow, the longitudinal slope of sidewalk ramps shall be ≤1:20. Smooth-surfaced ramp slabs shall be treated with anti-slip measures. Ramps that do not meet the requirements shall be demolished and reconstructed during rectification. 1.2 At-Grade Crossing System 1.2.1 Crossing at At-Grade Intersections 1. Basic Principles A. The slow-traffic organization for pedestrians and non-motor vehicles within grade-separated interchange areas shall be continuous, safe, and convenient, and should be arranged at ground level to avoid pedestrians and non-motor vehicles having to go up and down or increasing detour distances. 2. Quality Enhancement A. Reducing crossing distance Reducing the curb radius at intersections can effectively lower turning speeds, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, and enlarge pedestrian waiting areas. The facility strip or green belt along the roadside may also be appropriately used to create a pedestrian stopping space. Table 1.2-1 Recommended Curb Radius Values | Road class | Recommended curb radius (m) | |---|---:| | Main and secondary arterial roads | 5–10 | | Branch roads | 5–8 | Note: For exclusive right-turn lanes with traffic islands, the recommended curb radius is 8–10 m. Figure 1.2-1 Reducing Road Curb Radius B. Secondary crossing refuge island When the pedestrian or bicycle crossing traverses more than 4 lanes of two-way motor vehicle traffic, or when the crossing length exceeds 16 m, a secondary crossing refuge island shall be set in the center of the road. The island width shall not be less than 2 m, and in difficult circumstances not less than 1.5 m. On roads with a median strip (or where lane width can be reduced), pedestrian crossings on signal-free sections shall be provided with a “Z”-shaped secondary crossing refuge island. The refuge island length shall not be less than 8 m, and corresponding guardrails shall be installed. Figure 1.2-2 Schematic Diagram of a “Z”-Shaped Secondary Crossing Refuge Island I C. All-direction cross intersection For intersections surrounded by relatively dense commercial facilities and heavy pedestrian flows, an “all-direction cross intersection” may be used as appropriate. This not only improves pedestrian crossing efficiency, but also prevents interference between pedestrians and motor vehicles. D. Improving the experience of non-motor vehicle crossings Intersections with large non-motor vehicle crossing volumes should be equipped with dedicated non-motor vehicle signal lights. At branch-road intersections with heavy non-motor vehicle traffic, explore moving the non-motor vehicle crossing waiting area in front of the motor vehicle stop line and granting an early green signal priority.
